Longwire Antenna Length Calculator

A random wire fed through a 9:1 unun works best when its length is not close to a multiple of a half wavelength on the bands you use; at those lengths the impedance is very high. This calculator checks lengths against the broadcast bands you choose.

Why some lengths are worse

A wire that is a whole number of half wavelengths long presents a very high impedance at its end. A 9:1 unun matches it poorly there, so signals on that band drop. The calculator marks each band's half-wave multiples (with a 3% margin) and lists the lengths left over.

For receiving, these effects are modest; any wire beats a whip. If you can only fit one length, pick from the good ranges for the bands you listen to most, and keep the coax run from the unun to the radio so the noisy indoor section isn't part of the antenna. More in our longwire guide and apartment antenna options.

Frequently asked questions

What is a good random wire length for shortwave listening?

Lengths that avoid half-wave resonance on the bands you use. For 49–13 m, the calculator shows the clear ranges; 9 m (about 29–30 ft) and similar short lengths are common starting points for portables.

Do I need an unun for a longwire?

Not for a short wire clipped straight to a portable. For longer outdoor wires fed with coax, a 9:1 unun improves matching and keeps indoor noise out.
